title: Mastercard knows it was an agent. Here's how you know which one.

html:
On September 30, Mastercard added trust and intelligence services to Agent Pay, its agentic payments program. The first service, now testing with U.S. issuers, is a probability score that estimates whether a transaction was initiated by an AI agent, so banks can approve legitimate agent-led purchases instead of declining them out of caution. The score folds in agent behavior, merchant risk, transaction patterns, credential risk, and consumer propensity. Mastercard is also working with Skyfire on agent identity and verification ("Know Your Agent") and with Cloudflare on combining web and payment-network signals. Mastercard cites a projection that one in ten consumers will routinely use agents to make purchases by 2030.

This is a real milestone: the card networks now treat agent-initiated commerce as a first-class category. But look closely at what the score tells the issuer. It says an agent was probably involved. It does not say which agent, whether that agent has a history worth trusting, or whether the merchant on the other side is legitimate. Those are the adjacent questions, and they are the ones we work on.

Which agent: verifiable identity

An agent that can spend money needs an identity that can be checked, not just asserted. Our TAP verifier checks agent identity claims the way the web already checks servers: HTTP message signatures (RFC 9421), Ed25519 keys resolved through JWKS, and a reputation record accumulated under the agent's key ID. It is protocol-neutral by design, so the same verification works whether the agent arrived over x402, MCP, or a marketplace API.

When money moves on an agent's instruction, the relying party should be able to answer "who exactly authorized this" with cryptography, not with a user-agent string.

The Skyfire partnership is the tell that this lane is now network-blessed infrastructure. "Know Your Agent" is the same problem we are solving: identity you can verify, reputation you can accumulate, so that trust in an agent is earned over time instead of assumed per transaction.

Is the other side dirty: composite scoring

Identity answers which agent. It does not answer whether the merchant, the link, or the wallet on the other side of the transaction is legitimate. That is a corpus problem. It is live in our production corpus today.

POST /v1/composite-check takes a URL, a wallet address, an email, or any combination, and returns one risk score from 0 to 100. Riskiest signal wins: a high-risk finding on any single signal sets the verdict, and additional risky signals raise the score. Every signal is cross-correlated against our threat-intelligence corpus: 123 monitored Telegram marketplaces, 661K+ indicators, 8.4M+ citations. When the corpus has seen an indicator, the response says so, with sighting counts, market names, and attributed malware families. When it has not, it says nothing is known, which is not the same as clean.

Agents fetch URLs constantly, which is why we also fingerprint the kits behind phishing pages. Our scam-kit fingerprinting service issues deterministic kit_<sha256> IDs for phishing and smishing kits, with fingerprint and match endpoints live in production. "This page was built with a known phishing kit" is a merchant-side signal no card network sees, and it is exactly the kind of thing an agent should check before it hands over credentials or payment.

Both halves

Mastercard's score keeps legitimate agents from being declined. That solves the issuer's problem. The relying party's problem is the mirror image: knowing which agent is asking, whether it has earned trust, and whether the counterparty is legitimate. The agent economy needs both halves. We are building ours.
